## Research Proposal 

This document outlines a proposed research project designed to evaluate whether occupational mobility in Canada follows a cost-minimizing transport structure. Detailed construction of distance measures, calibration procedures, and diagnostic evidence are documented in an accompanying Methods Companion. The analysis requires access to unsuppressed linked 2016 and 2021 Census microdata available only through the Statistics Canada Virtual Data Lab (VDL). The project will develop, estimate, and rigorously test alternative distance-based models of occupational mobility, with the goal of informing both academic research and workforce policy.

Workforce development policies increasingly assume that workers can transition between occupations requiring similar skill sets. This assumption underlies a wide range of policy tools, including labour market forecasts, career navigation platforms, and reskilling initiatives designed to move workers into emerging occupations. In effect, many workforce development strategies implicitly rely on a model of occupational mobility structured by skill proximity.

Despite the central role of this assumption in policy design, there is limited direct evidence on whether occupational mobility actually follows this pattern. In practice, labour market transitions may also be shaped by institutional structures such as credential requirements, occupational hierarchies, and other barriers that restrict which transitions are feasible. If these institutional factors dominate mobility patterns, policies built on skill-based mobility assumptions may systematically overestimate the ease with which workers can move into new occupations.

This project addresses this gap by evaluating how well different notions of occupational distance explain observed mobility patterns. Specifically, the analysis compares skill-based distance measures derived from occupational task profiles with hierarchical measures based on the National Occupational Classification (NOC). By testing which notion of distance better rationalizes observed occupational transitions, the project provides direct evidence on whether widely used career pathway frameworks accurately reflect labour market dynamics.

The results will help inform the design of workforce planning tools and reskilling initiatives by clarifying the extent to which workers can realistically transition between occupations based on their existing skill sets, and the extent to which institutional barriers constrain those transitions.

# Introduction

Labour markets must continually reallocate workers as technological change, industry restructuring, and demographic shifts alter the demand for occupations. Observed occupational transitions reflect both changes in labour demand and the difficulty of transferring existing skills across occupations. Because changes in occupational employment mechanically induce inflows and outflows, raw transition patterns do not directly reveal mobility frictions.

This paper asks whether occupational mobility among workers with stable human capital follows the structure predicted by entropy-regularized optimal transport, and conditional on this structure, which notion of occupational distance best rationalizes observed transitions. The 2016–2021 Canadian Census period provides a useful setting to study this question because it includes the COVID-19 shock, which generated substantial contractions and expansions across sectors.

Consistent with evidence that workers tend to transition between occupations with similar task requirements [@gathmann2010general], we model occupational mobility as declining with distance in occupational space. Our framework embeds this idea in a multinomial logit random utility model and solves for equilibrium flows using entropy-regularized optimal transport.

Unlike prior work that evaluates occupational distance indirectly through wages or reduced-form elasticities, this paper tests whether a candidate distance metric rationalizes the full observed transition matrix conditional on origin and destination totals. With linked Census data, optimal transport becomes a falsifiable allocation benchmark rather than an imputation device.

We implement this approach by conditioning on observed occupational marginals and asking which transition matrix best reconciles the flows with the friction penalties implied by the distance matrix. The transport equilibrium can match the data only if workers disproportionately move between nearby occupations in the proposed distance metric; it cannot succeed merely by reproducing occupational growth or decline. We estimate an entropy-regularized version that allows decentralized choice while preserving the observed accounting constraints.

We partition workers according to whether their highest educational attainment increased between 2016 and 2021. For the stable attainment group, the origin occupation provides a clear signal of the worker’s location in skill space, and occupational distance is expected to rationalize mobility patterns. For example, a university professor with a Ph.D. in 2016 who becomes an economist with a Ph.D. in 2021 represents the type of transition that occupational distance can plausibly rationalize.

In contrast, for the attainment increase group, new training may allow workers to move to occupations that are quite distant from their original occupation. For example, a cashier with a B.Sc. in 2016 who becomes a physician in 2021 with an M.D. has acquired new human capital that permits such a large occupational jump. Occupational distances derived from the initial occupation will therefore struggle to rationalize this mobility. This group provides a structural contrast: if the framework captures the reallocation of fixed human capital, its fit should weaken.

This partition ignores new credentials that do not change an individual’s highest level of educational attainment. Such cases are relatively infrequent (n.b. should show using BC education data) and are less likely to substantially alter a worker’s human capital than the acquisition of a new highest credential.

The two groups likely differ in other ways as well, including age, career stage, and origin occupation. Comparisons across the groups are therefore not interpreted causally. Rather, the partition isolates a regime in which human capital is plausibly stable over the period, illustrating when a distance-based mobility model should perform well and when it is expected to fail. Differences in model performance may therefore reflect both the regime distinction and compositional differences, rather than the causal effect of increases in highest educational attainment. The comparison is intended to assess whether a distance-based model explains mobility when human capital is fixed, not whether education itself causes mobility to deviate from the model.

We evaluate whether mobility in the stable attainment group follows a cost-minimizing transport structure. Within this framework, we compare skill-based and hierarchical distance metrics and allow explanatory power to vary across destination education-gating regimes. If supported by the data, the results identify the economically relevant geometry of occupational distance and provide a disciplined framework for understanding labour-market adjustment.

The analysis proceeds in three steps. First, we evaluate whether occupational mobility among workers with stable human capital exhibits the exponential distance structure implied by entropy-regularized optimal transport. Second, we compare competing notions of occupational distance — skill similarity and hierarchical classification — and examine how their explanatory power varies across destination education-gating regimes. Third, we study workers who acquire new credentials between censuses to understand when education enables mobility that bypasses the distance constraints governing ordinary reallocation.

# Literature Review

Occupational mobility plays a central role in how labour markets reallocate workers when the structure of employment changes. A large labour economics literature studies mobility as an adjustment mechanism through which workers respond to economic shocks. A central finding is that mobility is constrained by the transferability of human capital across occupations: workers moving between similar occupations experience smaller earnings losses and transition more frequently than those switching to distant occupations.

Task-based approaches formalize this idea by representing occupations as bundles of tasks. @PoletaevRobinson2008 relate wage losses following displacement to changes in skill portfolios constructed from occupational descriptors. @GathmannSchoenberg2010 show that mobility probabilities decline with task distance and that career paths become increasingly localized as workers accumulate occupation-specific human capital. Subsequent work constructs empirical distance measures between occupations and interprets these distances as switching costs governing labour market adjustment.

However, observed mobility patterns reflect not only bilateral frictions but also equilibrium changes in occupational employment. Expanding occupations attract workers from many sources regardless of switching costs, so transition frequencies reflect both transition costs and demand-driven expansion. Understanding reallocation therefore requires modelling the joint allocation of flows across all occupations while conditioning on observed origin and destination totals.

Optimal transport provides a framework for modelling such reallocations under accounting constraints. Rather than modelling individual transitions independently, the allocation is characterized as a mass reallocation that minimizes total transition cost while preserving origin and destination totals. In economics, optimal transport has been applied to matching and assignment problems because it integrates cost structure with market-clearing conditions @Galichon2016. Classical optimal transport, however, yields deterministic allocations that concentrate mass on a small number of transitions.

Entropy-regularized optimal transport introduces dispersion and produces allocations of the form

$$
P_{ij} = u_i \exp(-C_{ij}/\varepsilon) v_j,
$$

which resemble discrete-choice probabilities while enforcing simultaneous origin and destination constraints. Computationally, this solution can be obtained using Sinkhorn scaling @Cuturi2013 and can be interpreted as a decentralized equilibrium reallocation mechanism rather than a planner’s assignment.

A related literature models flows using gravity equations, in which bilateral movements depend on distance and on origin and destination size, with general-equilibrium conditions ensuring aggregate consistency @AndersonVanWincoop2003; @HeadMayer2014. Entropic optimal transport can be viewed as a structural analogue in which the exponential cost kernel plays the role of distance and scaling factors endogenously satisfy observed marginals exactly. Unlike gravity regressions estimated bilaterally, the transport allocation is derived as the solution to a global minimization problem that enforces exact mass conservation.

Another literature studies how education shapes occupational mobility. Field-of-study mismatch research shows that specialized training concentrates workers into narrow occupation sets, while general education supports broader mobility. Measures of educational specificity capture the dispersion of graduates across occupations and predict mobility patterns. In a reallocation framework, these differences imply that education affects not only transition rates but whether occupational changes represent movement along an existing cost geometry or shifts to a new position within it.

This paper connects these literatures by modelling occupational flows as an equilibrium reallocation governed by a distance matrix and using education timing to identify when occupational distance should govern mobility. We evaluate which notion of occupational distance rationalizes aggregate flows and whether the same frictions govern worker-level mobility behavior across education-timing regimes.

# Aggregate mobility

We model occupational mobility as a reallocation problem conditional on observed employment changes. Because the number of workers leaving each occupation and entering each occupation must simultaneously hold, flows cannot be determined independently across occupation pairs. Instead, the pattern of replacement across occupations reflects the costs workers face when transferring existing human capital.

We begin from the canonical optimal transport formulation of labour reallocation. The optimal transport problem provides a convenient representation of the joint reallocation constraint: flows must satisfy origin and destination employment totals simultaneously while favoring lower-cost transitions.

Let $a$ denote the distribution of workers across occupations at time $t$, and $b$ the distribution at time $t+1$. Let $C_{ij}$ measure the difficulty of moving from occupation $i$ to $j$. The optimal transport allocation solves

$$
P^\star = \argmin_{P\in\Pi(a,b)} \sum_{ij} C_{ij}P_{ij}
$$

where $\Pi(a,b)=\{P\ge0: P\mathbf{1}=a,\;P^\top\mathbf{1}=b\}$.

Observed mobility reflects decentralized decisions by heterogeneous workers facing imperfect information and idiosyncratic preferences. Introducing an entropic perturbation yields the equilibrium allocation generated by random utility choice with occupation-specific fixed effects determined endogenously to satisfy labour-market clearing. Entropy-regularized optimal transport is equivalent to decentralized choice under logit frictions, making it a natural equilibrium benchmark for mobility decisions.

$$
P_\varepsilon = \argmin_{P\in\Pi(a,b)} \sum_{ij} C_{ij}P_{ij}+ \varepsilon \sum_{ij}P_{ij}(\log P_{ij}-1)
$$

This modification yields the solution

$$
P_{ij} = u_i\,e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}\,v_j
$$

where $e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}$ converts transition costs into choice probabilities. The scaling vectors $u_i$ and $v_j$ are endogenous adjustments ensuring that origin and destination employment totals are satisfied simultaneously. The parameter $\varepsilon$ governs substitution across occupations: larger values imply greater randomness in occupational choice, while smaller values imply sharper sorting into lower-cost transitions. The entropic transport solution is mathematically equivalent to a multinomial logit allocation in which transition probabilities decline exponentially with occupational distance, subject to origin and destination constraints. Under standard random utility models with i.i.d. extreme value shocks, such exponential decay in choice probabilities provides a microfoundation for the entropic transport formulation.

Note that as $\varepsilon \to 0$, the stochastic equilibrium converges to the minimum-cost reallocation benchmark:

$$
\lim_{\varepsilon\to0} P_\varepsilon = P^\star
$$

Thus, optimal transport provides a benchmark allocation, while the regularized problem describes a decentralized equilibrium with heterogeneous agents. We estimate the regularized model because it yields a continuous mapping from cost matrices to implied mobility and corresponds to a behavioral model of worker choice.

Because occupational growth and decline are imposed by construction, the model is evaluated on the composition of flows rather than on employment levels. With origin and destination totals fixed, distance can shape only bilateral substitution patterns among reallocating workers. This conditioning isolates the role of transition costs from changes in occupational employment and distinguishes the transport equilibrium from unconstrained gravity-style regressions that do not impose joint mass conservation.

## Relation to Gravity Models

The solution to the entropy-regularized transport problem takes the form

$$
P_{ij}^{\star} = a_i^{\star} b_j^{\star} \exp(-C_{ij}/\varepsilon)
$$

Taking logs yields

$$
\log P_{ij}^{\star} = \log a_i^{\star} + \log b_j^{\star} - C_{ij}/\varepsilon ,
$$

which is formally identical to a gravity model with origin and destination fixed effects.

The difference lies in identification. In gravity models the fixed effects and the cost parameter are estimated jointly. In the Sinkhorn formulation the margins are imposed as constraints, so candidate cost matrices are evaluated solely on their ability to rationalize the residual structure of flows.

We next construct candidate occupational distance measures that discipline substitution patterns in the transport model.

## Distance Metrics

The candidate distance matrices are constructed entirely from occupational descriptors and classification structure — including O*NET task vectors and the NOC hierarchy — and do not use observed Canadian worker transitions. They therefore impose economically motivated restrictions on substitution patterns rather than fitting bilateral flows. Because the transport model matches aggregate growth and decline by construction, empirical content lies in whether these externally defined proximity measures rationalize observed bilateral reallocation. The comparison thus constitutes an out-of-sample test of competing mobility mechanisms.

### Skill distance

We construct a skill-based occupational distance using the O\*NET database, which reports 161 descriptors covering skills, abilities, knowledge, and work activities. Because similarity measures behave poorly in very high dimensions—distances between occupations become nearly uniform—raw Euclidean distances would contain little economically meaningful variation. We therefore reduce dimensionality using principal components analysis. The first ten components explain over 80% of the variation in the O\*NET measures, indicating that most cross-occupation differences lie in a low-dimensional structure. Occupational distance is defined as Euclidean distance within this ten-dimensional subspace.

Seven NOCs lack a direct mapping to O\*NET occupations. For these cases, we assign skill vectors equal to the mean skill profile of their corresponding four-digit NOC group, preserving classification structure while avoiding arbitrary imputation. One occupation (44200: Primary combat members of the Canadian Armed Forces) lacks a corresponding four-digit aggregate and is therefore excluded.

### Hierarchical distance

The NOC classification provides an alternative notion of occupational proximity based on institutional and hierarchical structure rather than measured human capital similarity. NOC is a nested taxonomy in which additional digits progressively refine work descriptions along task, responsibility, and credential dimensions. In the 2021 classification, occupations are coded at five digits, with each additional digit representing a finer level of specialization.

The first digit defines broad occupational domains that typically correspond to distinct labour markets and credential systems; transitions across this level represent major career changes. The second digit records the Training, Education, Experience and Responsibilities (TEER) category, which orders occupations by required human capital depth and captures upgrading or downgrading in qualification intensity. The first three digits define major occupational groups sharing task domains and credential pathways, while the first four digits identify closely related occupations with substantial skill transferability. The five-digit code denotes the unit occupation.

The hierarchical metric exploits the nested structure of the NOC classification to proxy institutional and career-boundary frictions embedded in the taxonomy itself. Similarity between occupations is determined by the deepest level at which their codes coincide: divergence at earlier digits reflects separation across broad occupational domains, while divergence at later digits reflects finer specialization within a shared domain. Within major groups, differences in TEER capture vertical differentiation in required training intensity and responsibility. The resulting metric therefore encodes both horizontal specialization (through taxonomy depth) and vertical qualification differences (through TEER level) in a bounded and ordered scale.

Distance is defined by the level at which two occupations diverge. The scale is ordinal rather than cardinal: its role is to rank occupational separation rather than measure absolute retraining cost. Occupations sharing all five digits are assigned distance zero. If they share the first four digits, the distance is one; if they share the first three digits, the distance is two. If occupations share only the first digit, the distance equals three plus the absolute difference in TEER level. Because TEER ranges from 0 to 5, this implies a maximum within-major-group distance of eight. Occupations that differ in the first digit are assigned the maximal distance of nine. Large vertical differences within a domain can therefore approach the separation implied by cross-domain transitions, reflecting the interpretation that substantial qualification gaps may be nearly as binding as domain shifts.

Unlike the skill-based distance derived from O\*NET descriptors, this metric does not rely on continuous similarity in underlying abilities. Instead, it captures institutional segmentation arising from credential regimes, responsibility hierarchies, and broad occupational domains. Comparing the flow allocations implied by this metric to those generated by the skill distance allows us to assess whether observed mobility patterns are more consistent with transferable human capital or with hierarchical segmentation.

The hierarchical distance matrix is discrete and contains large plateaus of equal-cost occupation pairs. In classical (unregularized) optimal transport, such discreteness can generate multiple optimal plans and arbitrary mass splitting across equal-cost cells. Entropic regularization yields a unique transport plan with strictly positive support, implying that all occupation pairs receive some (potentially negligible) mass. Among occupation pairs with identical costs, mass is allocated in a maximum-entropy manner, so discreteness does not induce instability in the implied flow matrix.

### Regularization Calibration

As a baseline, we define “local” hierarchical mobility using the distribution of non-maximal hierarchical distances (excluding pairs at the maximal category distance). We take the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of this non-maximal distribution as alternative locality anchors. For each anchor value, we compute its percentile location within the full hierarchical distance distribution (including maximal-distance pairs), and apply that percentile to the skill-distance distribution to obtain a comparable characteristic skill cost. We then set the regularization parameter equal to the corresponding characteristic cost in each metric, so that the exponential kernel downweights a “typical local” move by a comparable factor across metrics. The objective is comparability across metrics, not structural estimation of $\varepsilon$.

This mapping ensures that regularization strength reflects comparable substitution margins across metrics, while allowing robustness to how “local” is defined within the informative region of the hierarchical metric. As a separate robustness check, we report sensitivity to proportional rescalings of $\varepsilon$ around each anchored baseline (e.g., multiplying by 0.5 and 2), holding the anchor definition fixed.

# Aggregate Results

We evaluate the transport model along four dimensions. The null hypothesis is that, conditional on origin and destination totals, bilateral flows are unrelated to occupational distance. In the entropic transport framework, this corresponds to the high-temperature limit in which $\varepsilon \rightarrow \infty$, and the flow matrix converges to the maximum-entropy allocation $P_{ij} = a_i b_j$: distance plays no role. The alternative is that flows decline exponentially with distance, as implied by the entropy-regularized transport structure.

## Does the exponential distance structure describe observed flows?

Under entropic transport, log excess transition probability declines linearly with distance. This implies an exponential relationship between flows and distance and restricts dispersion among occupation pairs with identical costs. We therefore test whether observed flows exhibit this exponential structure rather than merely declining monotonically with distance. Large heterogeneity among equal-cost pairs or systematic curvature inconsistent with the log-linear form would constitute evidence against the model.

## Which distance metric better captures mobility frictions?

We compare model-implied and observed bilateral flows under alternative distance matrices. Because origin and destination marginals are imposed, evaluation focuses exclusively on the composition of flows across occupation pairs. The preferred metric is the one whose implied allocation most closely approximates the observed transition matrix according to Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence.

## Is there heterogeneity by destination education gating intensity?

Occupational transitions may be governed by different frictions across segments of the labour market. In particular, occupations vary in the extent to which entry is tightly linked to specific educational credentials.

To capture this heterogeneity, we construct a size-adjusted measure of **destination education gating intensity** based on the KL divergence between the education distribution within each occupation and the overall education distribution of the workforce.

For each occupation $n$, let $p(e \mid n)$ denote the distribution of highest-attained education and field of study among workers in that occupation, and let $p(e)$ denote the corresponding distribution in the labour market as a whole. We define occupational gating intensity as

$$
D_{KL}(p(e \mid n) \parallel p(e)).
$$

Because divergence increases mechanically in small occupations, we residualize $\log D_{KL}$ with respect to occupation size. The resulting measure captures how unusually concentrated an occupation’s educational pipeline is, conditional on scale. The measure captures concentration in educational pipelines and may reflect both formal credential requirements and historical sorting patterns rather than purely institutional barriers.

We partition destination occupations into high- and low-gating groups using a pre-specified median split and evaluate model performance separately within each regime. If mobility into education-gated occupations is primarily constrained by institutional and credential barriers, hierarchical distance should better rationalize flows into high-gating destinations. Conversely, if mobility into open-entry occupations reflects transferable human capital, skill-based distance should better rationalize flows into low-gating destinations.

The regularization parameter is held fixed across distance metrics and destination regimes so that differences in model performance reflect cost structure rather than parameter tuning. The regularization parameter is fixed prior to model comparison and is not tuned to maximize fit for any specific distance metric.

## Does the model primarily describe *stable attainment* group?

The transport mechanism is intended to describe reallocation of existing human capital. We therefore estimate the model separately for the *stable attainment* and *attainment increase* groups. If mobility following credential attainment reflects sorting into newly accessible occupations rather than friction-constrained reallocation, the transport structure should weaken in that group. We now turn to cases where human capital changes between censuses, and mobility may bypass these distance frictions.

# Individual mobility

If occupational mobility primarily reflects reallocation of fixed human capital, the transport framework should describe most worker transitions. However, *attainment increase* may allow workers to bypass these frictions. The individual-level analysis therefore examines the circumstances under which workers make large occupational jumps that violate the distance-based mobility structure.

We hypothesize that two characteristics are associated with larger occupational jumps. The first is the occupational specificity of an educational program, defined as how concentrated a program’s graduates are across occupations relative to the overall education distribution. The second is the educational specificity of destination occupations, defined as how concentrated an occupation’s entrants are across programs relative to the overall employment distribution. Highly specific educational programs and strongly gated occupations both create targeted entry pathways that allow workers to bypass the gradual occupational adjustments implied by distance-based mobility.

Both measures are constructed from the 2021 Census NOC–CIP–attainment table, rather than the linked census microdata used to measure occupational transitions.

To account for differences in starting positions within occupational space, the regressions include origin occupation fixed effects (2-digit NOC). These controls help block potential confounding between the distance traveled and the individual's choice of education.

## Education Specificity

We construct a **size-adjusted measure of education specificity** using a cross-tabulation of field of study (CIP), highest attainment, and occupation (NOC). This measure is the flip side of destination gating which was described in the aggregate mobility section.  The objective here is to quantify how informative a given education is about occupational outcomes. Occupational distributions are inferred from finite counts, and small cells (fewer than ten individuals) are suppressed, causing traditional concentration measures (e.g., Herfindahl–Hirschman Index, entropy, support size) to depend mechanically on sample size rather than true specialization.

We instead measure how distinct an education’s occupational distribution is from the overall labour market distribution using Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. For each field-of-study × attainment group $e$, let $p_e(n)$ denote the share of workers employed in occupation $n$, and let $p_0(n)$ denote the occupational distribution of the educated workforce as a whole. Educational specificity is defined as

$$
D_{KL}(p_e \parallel p_0)
=
\sum_n p_e(n)\,\log\!\left(\frac{p_e(n)}{p_0(n)}\right),
$$

which measures how much knowing an individual’s education shifts expectations about their occupation. Higher values indicate concentration in a distinct set of occupations, while values near zero correspond to diffuse, general education. Because each term is weighted by observed probability mass, small or suppressed cells contribute little to the statistic, making the measure robust to discretization and censoring.

Raw divergence nevertheless increases mechanically for small groups. We therefore residualize $\log D_{KL}$ with respect to group size using an OLS regression of log divergence on log group size, yielding a size-adjusted index that captures occupational distinctiveness rather than sampling noise. The resulting measure reflects how strongly an education channels workers into particular occupations and serves as our measure of educational specificity.

## Regression specification

To examine the determinants of education-enabled occupational jumps, we estimate a regression relating the distance between an individual’s 2016 and 2021 occupations to measures of educational specificity and destination gating. The sample is restricted to individuals whose most recent educational attainment occurs between the 2016 and 2021 censuses.

The baseline specification is

$$
d_i = \alpha + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 G_i + \beta_3 (S_i \times G_i) + \gamma_{o(i)} + \varepsilon_i
$$


where $d_i$ denotes the occupational distance traveled between 2016 and 2021 for individual $i$. Distances are measured separately using the skill-based metric derived from O*NET and the hierarchical distance derived from the NOC classification. 

The variable $S_i$ represents the size-adjusted **education specificity** of the individual’s most recent field-of-study $\times$ attainment group, constructed from the 2021 Census CIP--NOC--attainment table. Higher values indicate educational programs whose graduates are concentrated in a narrower set of occupations.

The variable $G_i$ represents the **destination gating** measure for the individual’s 2021 occupation. This measure captures the extent to which entry into a given occupation is concentrated among a narrow set of educational programs.

The term $\gamma_{o(i)}$ denotes **origin occupation fixed effects** at the 2-digit NOC level. These controls account for differences in workers’ starting positions within occupational space, ensuring that identification comes from comparisons among workers beginning in similar parts of the labour market.

A positive coefficient on education specificity would indicate that more targeted educational programs are associated with larger occupational jumps. A positive coefficient on destination gating would indicate that entry into more tightly credentialed occupations is associated with larger jumps. A positive interaction term would suggest that the largest movements occur when highly specific programs channel workers into strongly gated occupations.






# Anticipated Contributions and Interpretation

If supported by the data, the project would provide evidence that occupational mobility in Canada can be represented as structured reallocation governed by measurable frictions. Specifically, the analysis clarifies (i) whether mobility patterns are better explained by continuous similarity in measured skills and abilities or by hierarchical segmentation embedded in the occupational taxonomy, and (ii) whether the relevance of these friction structures varies systematically with destination education-gating intensity.

The comparison across education-timing regimes further distinguishes between reallocation of existing human capital and assignment following new credential acquisition, separating friction-constrained switching from credential-driven entry.

From a policy perspective, the results inform whether workforce adjustment policies should emphasize skill transferability, credential pathways, or institutional barriers. Academically, the project integrates optimal transport theory, educational specificity, and linked Census microdata within a unified empirical framework, advancing optimal transport as an empirically testable model of labour-market frictions.

The research design articulates falsifiable implications at both aggregate and individual levels. Failure of flows to exhibit the exponential distance structure implied by the model, absence of educational specificity gradients, or inconsistency between macro and micro evidence would weaken the transport interpretation and guide refinement of the framework.

The 2016–2021 period provides a stringent test because it includes a large aggregate shock. If a structured cost geometry governs reallocation during this episode, similar substitution patterns should characterize more gradual periods, even if the magnitude of churn and dispersion varies across macroeconomic environments.
